items.title: 给 Claude Code 点「允许」一天要切几十次窗口，我把它搬到灵动岛上了
items.author: wxgj2001
items.text:
给 Claude Code 点「允许」这件事，一天要切几十次窗口。我把它搬到灵动岛上了。
平时我同时开好几个 AI 编码代理：Claude Code 两三个会话、Cursor 一个窗口。
烦的不是启动它们，是每次要写文件、跑命令，都得停下来等我批准：
切窗口 → 找到那个终端 → 看清楚它想干嘛 → 点允许 → 再切回来
一天几十次，节奏全碎。
所以写了个工具，把这些代理收进屏幕顶部一个灵动岛里：
要权限时，岛上直接出现「允许 / 拒绝」
代理提问时，按 ⌘1 / ⌘2 选
审阅计划，也是在岛上过
点一下，跳回对应的 iTerm2 标签页
顺带能看到谁在跑、谁卡住、谁在等你
原生 Swift，四个代理挂着大概 40MB。面板是非激活窗口，点它不会抢走编辑器的焦点，拖到副屏会自己跟过去。
代理走的是各家自己的 hooks / settings，内置 30 来个：Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Trae、Windsurf、Cline……
有几个我还在逐个验证，README 里列了每个的真实状态。
现在限时免费，领个永久激活码就行，最多 3 台设备。不领码也能先试用 14 天。
https://imagentx.top/products/xisland
先说两个坑，免得你白折腾：
目前是 adhoc 签名，没买苹果开发者证书。第一次打开若提示「已损坏」，在终端跑一下：
xattr -cr "/Applications/X Island.app"
只支持 macOS 13 以上。
想听听大家平时的用法：你们是开多个会话并行，还是一个会话干到底？

items.title: 我运营着好几个站，最后还是自己写了个 CMS
items.author: holyxing
items.text:
我运营着好几个站，最烦的不是写稿，是每个站各装一套后台、插件和更新。最后还是自己写了个 CMS：一个后台管所有站，发布即静态，AI 写作在编辑器里，一条命令自托管。
一个后台管所有站，不是一套系统管一个站。运营几个内容站的人最痛的不是写稿，是运维：5 个站就是 5 套后台、5 套插件、5 份更新和备份，改一个全站通用的东西要登 5 次后台点 5 遍。AI-CMS 把站点、栏目、内容、媒体、版式收进同一个后台，带 RBAC 权限和回收站，加新站是点几下的事，不是再装一套系统。版式那层也做到了可管：HTML 模板用 HY_ 标签，带版本管理和资产依赖，还能按全站、栏目、详情三级作用域分别生效，改版不用提心吊胆，也不用为每个站各养一套前台。
发布即静态，改一篇文章不用全站重建。内容发布时生成 Astro 静态站，CDN 直达读者。动态后台只在写稿时用，线上跑的是静态文件：打开快，而且线上根本没有动态后台可供攻击，攻击面小得多。构建粒度可以细到站点、栏目、单篇文章，改一篇文章只重建这一篇，不用全站重来。发布成败和耗时都会进铃铛中心告诉你，运维的人不用猜。
AI 写作在编辑器里，不在另一个标签页。很多 CMS 的 AI 是外挂一个聊天框，写一段、复制一段、粘贴回来再排版，切换成本全在用户身上。AI-CMS 的 AI 助手长在编辑器里：起草、改写、润色直接对正文动手，还有上下文感知的快捷操作，覆盖文章、模板和通用对话；增强工具包括文风清理、润色和图片本地化。Provider 可插拔，OpenAI 兼容接口、Anthropic 、MiniMax 、Ollama 本地模型都能接，API Key…

items.title: 嫌 Playwright 发小红书 / 抖音要天天维护 Cookie？我做了个 Chrome 扩展 + Native Messaging 的多平台分发工具，支持 Claude Code Skill
items.author: gybin02
items.text:
我是开发者，分享一个自己在用的工具：快推 EasyPost 。
痛点很直接：用 Playwright / Puppeteer 这类无头浏览器发视频，要配 Python 环境、下浏览器、手动导出 Cookie ，Cookie 一过期就得重来，还容易被平台识别成自动化脚本，滑块和验证码一卡就是半天。
EasyPost 换了一条路，不走无头浏览器：
跑在创作者日常用的真实 Chrome 里，复用浏览器当前登录态，不导出 Cookie 、不向工具交账号密码；
CLI 通过 Chrome Native Messaging 跟扩展通信，扩展在 Isolated World 里填内容；
fill 模式是自动填好标题、正文、标签和素材，最后一步发布由自己真鼠标点，发布前可以核对。
README 里的平台矩阵包括小红书、抖音、微信视频号、B 站、快手、微博、X 、Instagram ，CLI 是纯 JSON 输入输出，也带了 Agent Skill ，可以这样装：
npx skills add gybin02/easypost --skill easypost
开源部分是 MIT ，CLI 、Skills 和文档在仓库里，仓库 docs/ 下有 anti-risk-principles.md 、rpa-vs-extension.md 、tools-comparison.md 三篇横评，讲了和 Playwright 、传统 RPA 的架构差异。
提醒一句：这只是降低被识别为自动化脚本的概率，不是零风险，仍需遵守各平台规则，内容也请只发自己的或已授权的。

items.title: [iOS] 做了个「超级无聊」的跑步游戏：累计跑满 72 小时到终点，不动路就往回退
items.author: 1024ba
items.text:
大家好，我是这个 App 的开发者，来分享一个自己做的 iOS 小游戏：《跑不完》（英文名 The 72: Still Not There ）。免费下载，没有广告，不用注册。
规则只有一条：累计跑满 72 小时，到终点
是累计，不是连续。今天走 20 分钟、明天跑 1 小时，都会算进去。
停下来有宽限期：双腿模式 6 小时，手指模式 8 小时。
过了宽限期，路会慢慢往回退，每小时退 1 分钟。
连续 48 小时不动，就开始「崩塌」：每小时退 10 分钟，一直退回原点。
没有关卡，没有升级，没有每日任务。路就是一条很平淡的路。
两种跑法
双腿：用 iPhone 自带的计步，按 5 分钟一段判断你是不是在走或跑。App 不用一直开着，下次打开会把这段时间补算进来。也可以选择从 Apple 健康读步数，默认关闭。
手指：App 开在前台，按住屏幕就算在跑。每隔 3 到 8 分钟会有一只骆驼来挡路，20 秒内把它划走，不然就算你停了。iPad 上只有这个模式。
路上有什么
昼夜变化、天气、节日路牌边框；一共两条路线。
每跑 1 小时路过一块路牌，路过的路牌都收进收藏册。偶尔会遇到稀有的「路边目击」，比如一只热气球。
一个嘴有点毒的旁白：只吐槽行为，不评价人。你休息、暂停的时候，它会好好说话。

items.title: I am working on a Rust-based ext4 driver.
items.author: jfrei
items.text:
I am working on a Rust-based ext4 driver. The idea is that it can be re-used as a FUSE-based driver as well as (Windows) kernel driver (eventually).
Most of the essential features are implemented so far, but some (mandatory) features are lacking (xattrs support). My goal is to get to a full ext4 implementation that also supports ext2 and ext3 read/write.
The initial motivation was to have a pet project with a use-case for Rust, as I wanted to improve my Rust coding skills, after I did some work on a game server implementation in Rust earlier [1].
My goal is to have an implementation where I have digested every line mentally, which is something that pretty much excludes slop-like use of AI for large scale code generation. And of course I want to really trust the code that touches my files via raw hard disk access.
Hence, I use AI mainly for unit tests and (scoped) code rewriting when my code gets too verbose and cumbersome.
In the long run I'd want to add fuzzing to the implementation, so if anyone has experience on this, I'd be interested in getting some pointers.
[1] https://github.com/MordorWide/EANation

items.title: I've been working on a voxel game engine called Bonsai for ~10 years.
items.author: jesse__
items.text:
I've been working on a voxel game engine called Bonsai for ~10 years.
Probably the most interesting thing about it at the moment is the editor. The world, and most things in it, are represented as collections of SDFs. More accurately, they're density fields, but, potato-tomato. The world generator and editor operate almost entirely on the GPU. I've been writing a graph compiler similar in spirit to compilers that execute LLMs, with some key differences. The SDF 'program' gets jitted into a kind of bytecode and fed through an interpreter in the world gen shader. This way, the world gen and edits can be applied deterministically using one big fused program, and transferred back to CPU land using the async PCIe hardware. I get something on the order of ~99% ALU residency, 95% L2 hit rate and 20-40% vram bandwidth usage.
Compared to doing world gen on the CPU, it's so fast it feels like magic. It's taken me the better part of two years to get this working well.

items.title: 怎么才能用 ai 搜索到更多的情报呢
items.author: koukyo
items.text:
我发现一个很大的问题，大家包括我都会觉得 agent 搜索的能力很强，遇到什么事情就会让其进行调研
诚然 agent 能解决多数时候的浅搜索，但诸如“想要找到尽可能多的被动收入开发者平台”这样的问题，ai 似乎只会给几个出名的大平台，让人不是很满意。
到底是什么导致了这个问题呢，我和 gemini-4 聊了聊，意识到这是 agent 的 search 工具的缘故，其基本遵循了搜索引擎的最优结果。这就导致了 seo 做的好的平台也会被 search 推荐，agent 给出的结果也就只剩下大平台了。
不过，seo 好的结果并不一定是我们需要的结果，正如我上面举的找被动收入平台的例子
那怎么才能拖出 seo 进行搜索呢？我了解到市面上有一些网页向量搜索产品（这里不具体推荐），能够返回和标的网页语意相似度高的页面
于是我设计一个如下流程，能某种程度缓解信息的集中。应该在想要尽可能发散搜索消息时很有用，即
根网页->向量搜索 N 个相似的网页->AI 筛选和意图相关的 n 个网页->继续基于这 n 个网页进行向量搜索扩展
我测试了找被动收入平台的例子，找到了几十个可能有关的网站，部分甚至刚准备上线或者还处于测试阶段。这满足了我对这个 case 的期待。
来这分享给大家，说不定有些许启发

items.title: 让 Ai 的语气更灵动活泼， tone-particles：给 AI 加一点人味
items.author: shenyin
items.text:
和 AI 聊久了会发现一个问题：它答得都对，就是太"平淡"了。每句话都工整、礼貌、无懈可击，像一份永远不出错的说明书。
于是做了 tone-particles （语气助词 Skill ）——不改回答内容，只给表达层加一点口吻。
内置 21 种中文风格：御姐、萌妹、傲娇、高冷、三无、知性、学姐、老师、大小姐……搭配四种运行模式——固定一种、加权融合、随机轮换、融合随机，再加密度调节和颜文字开关，同一套答案能在不同语气间自由切换。截图里那句"唔，表哥，更新好啦～"，就是它跑起来的样子。
但它不是简单"换个皮"。核心原则叫先答后套：助词只作用于表达层，不进入代码块、表格、数字和专有名词，技术内容一字不差。碰到代码、报错排查、正式写作或情绪低落，它会自动降档；出现危机信号则完全关闭风格。连随机都由脚本按 seed 抽样，可复现、不失控。

items.title: I started as a dev shop and built 2 API products based on user demand.
items.author: Bencheng
items.text:
I started as a dev shop and built 2 API products based on user demand.
1 is an OCR and document extraction service [0]. We started with three customers asking for the same services and found none that were really useful (and supported Chinese characters) on the market at that time. Lately the product pivoted to based on (fine-tuned) LLM/VLMs and focus on adding various features that LLM out of the box are missing (fine tune based on specific customers data, prompt tune for particular type of elements e.g. Checkboxes, split 100s pages of PDF into dozens of documents with a few pages)
We're at around 55k MRR, the price model is per page, and we sign annual contracts with most clients (with some discounts)
2nd is an open-source CIAM [1]; Around 35k MRR.
We knew nothing about marketing when we started, so we partnered with local GCP/Azure as an ISV to get our first paying customers, which drove us to the more "Corporate" segment of the market.
A huge challenge is obviously how to market the product, but customer support for developers is tough as well -- you have to be developers to provide support for other developers, and sometimes it feels like you're troubleshooting for another dev…

items.title: We run an API to finetune text-to-image models (dreamlook.ai), as a two-person team.
items.author: MasterScrat
items.text:
We run an API to finetune text-to-image models (dreamlook.ai), as a two-person team.
When we launched 3 years ago our differentiator was that we could train both cheaper and faster by running on TPUs, these days GPUs have mostly caught up, and open source models are not as competitive as they once were.
It’s making ~5k/month these days, not bad as we’re no longer actively working on it, but a fraction of what we were doing a year ago.
The main challenge for us was the non-technical part. We built an API-first product because we love the tech and felt it’d allow us to focus on that part. But we still had to do marketing, sales support etc which we didn’t enjoy or excel at.
Now we’re both back in larger companies where we can focus on doing ML. It was satisfying to build a working business from scratch, no regrets, but I’m definitely happier now.

items.title: I make a living from the SMS & telephony API I made.
items.author: jlundberg
items.text:
I make a living from the SMS & telephony API I made.
Our MRR is ~500 000 EUR and our pricing model is pay-as-you-go (per SMS, per MMS, per phone call minute, per month for virtual mobile phone numbers).
The problem we solve is programmatic access to the mobile networks, specifically in Europe/Sweden.
We got out first paying customers through offline networking: going to hackathons, meetups and poking tech friends to find the first few early adopters.
Which is also our biggest challenge, it is hard to scale an offline based go-to-market method.
It has certainly been a painful struggle to get here and it still feels surreal it works so well.

I work for a tiny company. Most of the revenue is from paid API access.
I don't think I'm authorized to share any of the specifics, so will keep it generic.
The API is a world-class machine learning model for a specific scenario. There's a public price list, and various customers manage to negotiate various discounts.
Our biggest challenge is that Google Lens (while much worse than us for our specific domain) is becoming good enough for the average potential customer.
I think one of the regrets is only doing the ML API and not the end-user apps. It turns out the people creating the front end pocket most of the money.

items.title: Not making a living, but I make about $200/mo from an API that parses recipe ingredients like "2 cu…
items.author: mtlynch
items.text:
Not making a living, but I make about $200/mo from an API that parses recipe ingredients like "2 cups finely chopped onions" into structured JSON.[0]
I put it in maintenance mode in 2019, so it's about 99% passive income, as I spend only about an hour or two on maintenance per year.
I'm surprised all my clients haven't switched to LLMs, but maybe I still outdo LLMs on price/accuracy since it's so niche.
I'd like to sell it to someone who wants to do something with it, but it would probably take me 30-40 hours to package everything up to hand off to someone, so I consider just the opportunity cost there to be around $5-10k, and I don't think anyone wants to pay $10k for an API that makes $200/mo.
What I wish I knew: don't use RapidAPI. They charge 20%, they have a terrible interface, and they let customers run up huge charges and walk away without paying anything. I wish I'd just rolled my own simple thing with Paddle.
[0] https://zestfuldata.com/

items.title: I know of a guy, but his scenario was quite unique.
items.author: Simon_O_Rourke
items.text:
I know of a guy, but his scenario was quite unique. I was working for an energy company who shall remain nameless, but who's internal IT was a tangle of external consultants milking the place for millions, and ineffective/underserved full time staff who couldn't run a query on a database without a change control committee of consultants milking them for yet more cash.
Anyway, this guy was the go to guy for gas customers, and knew the database inside and out. So he created his own company, resigned as a full time employee, waited until the panic had set in properly.
Then he offered consulting services back to the energy company saying he'd take care of any database processing costs, or cloud migration costs or whatever, and moved the customer data for gas customers to his own system. Then he created an API, waited a while more and said he was going away again.... Or he could stay supporting this setup if the energy company agreed to a monthly fee and API usage. Then, as far as I know, he sat back and just watched the money roll in while he automated everything else about the job.

items.title: pioneer.app in their group-weekly update mode was the closest thing to early indie hackers.
items.author: authorfly
items.text:
pioneer.app in their group-weekly update mode was the closest thing to early indie hackers. Sadly they shut down that mechanism, I don't know why.
It was great for weekly reality checks but also UI and headline help.
That said, I had a FOMO of the "YC-access" and so I chose to spend B2B money with other companies at the startup stage (I know, foolish move). I spent a lot of money on Banana.dev, and helped their cofounders with feedback around concurrency/load for the API. Right as we gained some traction, they doubled prices, then changed the pricing model to make it unaffordable for us to run on their services. Felt a little nasty. And recently their pricing hit "you can only afford this if you already have VC level money"(probably to thin customers to a profitable subset).
